{{Short description|Group with no large product-free subset}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''quasirandom group''' is a [[group (mathematics)|group]] that does not contain a large product-free{{huh|date=April 2025}} [[subset]]. Such groups are precisely those without a small non-trivial [[irreducible representation]]. The namesake of these groups stems from their connection to [[graph theory]]: [[bipartite graph|bipartite]] [[Cayley graph]]s over any subset of a quasirandom group are always bipartite [[pseudorandom graph | quasirandom graphs]].

{{TOC left}}
{{clear}}

== Motivation ==

The notion of quasirandom groups arises when considering subsets of groups for which no two elements in the subset have a product in the subset; such subsets are termed <em>product-free</em>. [[László Babai]] and [[Vera Sós]] asked about the existence of a constant <math>c</math> for which every finite group <math>G</math> with order <math>n</math> has a product-free subset with size at least <math>cn</math>.<ref>{{citation | first1 = László | last1 = Babai|authorlink1 = László Babai | last2= Sós | first2 = Vera T.| authorlink2 = Vera T. Sós | title = Sidon sets in groups and induced subgraphs of Cayley graphs| journal = [[European Journal of Combinatorics]] | volume = 6 | year =1985 | issue = 2|pages = 101–114 |doi=10.1016/S0195-6698(85)80001-9 |doi-access=}}</ref> A well-known result of [[Paul Erdős]] about sum-free sets of integers can be used to prove that <math display="inline">c = \frac{1}{3}</math> suffices for [[abelian group]]s, but it turns out that such a constant does not exist for [[non-abelian group]]s.<ref>{{citation | first = P. | last = Erdős | authorlink = Paul Erdős | chapter = Extremal problems in number theory | title= Proceedings of the Symp. Pure Math. VIII|  publisher = American Mathematical Society | year = 1965 |pages = 181–189}}</ref>

Both non-trivial lower and upper bounds are now known for the size of the largest product-free subset of a group with order <math>n</math>. A lower bound of <math display="inline">cn^{\frac{11}{14}}</math> can be proved by taking a large subset of a union of sufficiently many [[cosets]],<ref>{{citation| first = Kiran S. |last = Kedlaya | authorlink = Kiran Kedlaya | title = Large product-free subsets of finite groups| journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series=Series A |volume = 77 | year = 1997 |issue = 2 | pages = 339–343 |doi=10.1006/jcta.1997.2715 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and an upper bound of <math display="inline">cn^{\frac{8}{9}}</math> is given by considering the [[projective special linear group]] <math>\operatorname{PSL}(2, p)</math> for any [[Prime number|prime]] <math>p</math>.<ref name = "g">{{citation | last = Gowers |first= W.T. | authorlink = Timothy Gowers | year = 2008 | title =  Quasirandom Groups | journal = Combinatorics, Probability and Computing | volume = 17 | issue = 3 | pages = 363–387| doi = 10.1017/S0963548307008826}}</ref> In the process of proving the upper bound, [[Timothy Gowers]] defined the notion of a quasirandom group to encapsulate the product-free condition and proved equivalences involving quasirandomness in graph theory.

== Graph quasirandomness ==
{{Main|Pseudorandom graph}}

Formally, it does not make sense to talk about whether or not a single group is quasirandom. The strict definition of quasirandomness will apply to [[sequences]] of groups, but first bipartite graph quasirandomness must be defined. The motivation for considering sequences of groups stems from its connections with [[graphon]]s, which are defined as limits of graphs in a certain sense.

Fix a real number <math>p \in [0, 1].</math> A sequence of bipartite graphs <math>(G_n)</math> (here <math>n</math> is allowed to skip integers as long as <math>n</math> tends to infinity) with <math>G_n</math> having <math>n</math> vertices, vertex parts <math>A_n</math> and <math>B_n</math>, and <math>(p + o(1)) | A_n | | B_n |</math> edges is '''quasirandom''' if any of the following equivalent conditions hold:

* For every bipartite graph <math>H</math> with vertex parts <math>A'</math> and <math>B'</math>, the number of labeled copies of <math>H</math> in <math>G_n</math> with <math>A'</math> embedded in <math>A</math> and <math>B'</math> embedded in <math>B</math> is <math display="inline">\left(p^{e(H)} + o(1)\right) | A | ^ {| A' |} | B | ^ {| B' |}.</math> Here, the function <math>o(1)</math> is allowed to depend on <math>H.</math>
* The number of [[Cycle (graph theory) | closed, labeled walks]] of length 4 in <math>G_n</math> starting in <math>A_n</math> is <math>(p^4 + o(1))| A_n |^2 | B_n |^2.</math>
* The number of edges between <math>A'</math> and <math>B'</math> is <math>p | A' | | B' | + n^2 o(1)</math> for any pair of subsets <math>A' \subseteq A_n</math> and <math>B' \subseteq B_n.</math>
* <math>\sum\limits_{a_1, a_2 \in A_n} N(a_1, a_2)^2 = (p^4 + o(1)) | A_n |^2 | B_n |^2</math>, where <math>N(u, v)</math> denotes the number of common [[Neighbourhood (graph theory) | neighbors]] of <math>u</math> and <math>v.</math>
* <math>\sum\limits_{b_1, b_2 \in B_n} N(b_1, b_2)^2 = (p^4 + o(1)) | A_n |^2 | B_n |^2.</math>
* The largest [[eigenvalue]] of <math>G_n</math>'s [[adjacency matrix]] is <math display="inline">(p + o(1)) \sqrt{| A | | B |}</math> and all other eigenvalues have magnitude at most <math display="inline">\sqrt{| A | | B |}o(1).</math>

It is a result of Chung–Graham–Wilson that each of the above conditions is equivalent.<ref>{{citation | last1 = Chung | first1 = F. R. K. | authorlink1 = Fan Chung | last2 =  Graham | first2 = R. L. | authorlink2 = Ronald Graham | last3 = Wilson | first3 = R. M. | authorlink3 = R. M. Wilson| year = 1989 | title = Quasi-Random Graphs | journal = Combinatorica | volume = 9 | issue = 4 | pages = 345–362 | doi = 10.1007/BF02125347 | s2cid = 17166765}}</ref> Such graphs are termed quasirandom because each condition asserts that the quantity being considered is approximately what one would expect if the bipartite graph was generated according to the [[Erdős–Rényi model | Erdős–Rényi random graph model]]; that is, generated by including each possible edge between <math>A_n</math> and <math>B_n</math> independently with probability <math>p.</math>

Though quasirandomness can only be defined for sequences of graphs, a notion of <math>c</math>-quasirandomness can be defined for a specific graph by allowing an error tolerance in any of the above definitions of graph quasirandomness. To be specific, given any of the equivalent definitions of quasirandomness, the <math>o(1)</math> term can be replaced by a small constant <math>c > 0</math>, and any graph satisfying that particular modified condition can be termed <math>c</math>-quasirandom. It turns out that <math>c</math>-quasirandomness under any condition is equivalent to <math>c^k</math>-quasirandomness under any other condition for some absolute constant <math>k \geq 1.</math>

The next step for defining group quasirandomness is the Cayley graph. Bipartite Cayley graphs give a way from translating quasirandomness in the graph-theoretic setting to the group-theoretic setting.

Given a finite group <math>\Gamma</math> and a subset <math>S \subseteq \Gamma</math>, the '''bipartite Cayley graph''' <math>\operatorname{BiCay}(\Gamma, S)</math> is the bipartite graph with vertex sets <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, each labeled by elements of <math>G</math>, whose edges <math>a \sim b</math> are between vertices whose ratio <math>ab^{-1}</math> is an element of <math>S.</math>

== Definition ==

With the tools defined above, one can now define group quasirandomness. A sequence of groups <math>(\Gamma_n)</math> with <math>| \Gamma_n | = n</math> (again, <math>n</math> is allowed to skip integers) is '''quasirandom''' if for every real number <math>p \in [0, 1]</math> and choice of subsets <math>S_n \subseteq \Gamma_n</math> with <math>| S_n | = (p + o(1)) | \Gamma_n |</math>, the sequence of graphs <math>\operatorname{BiCay}(\Gamma_n, S_n)</math> is quasirandom.<ref name="g"/>

Though quasirandomness can only be defined for sequences of groups, the concept of <math>c</math>-quasirandomness for specific groups can be extended to groups using the definition of <math>c</math>-quasirandomness for specific graphs.

== Properties ==

As proved by Gowers, group quasirandomness turns out to be equivalent to a number of different conditions.

To be precise, given a sequence of groups <math>(\Gamma_n)</math>, the following are equivalent:

* <math>(\Gamma_n)</math> is quasirandom; that is, all sequences of Cayley graphs defined by <math>(\Gamma_n)</math> are quasirandom.
* The dimension of the smallest non-trivial representation of <math>\Gamma_n</math> is unbounded.
* The size of the largest product-free subset of <math>\Gamma_n</math> is <math>o(| \Gamma_n |).</math>
* The size of the smallest non-trivial [[Quotient group | quotient]] of <math>\Gamma_n</math> is unbounded.<ref name="g"/>

Cayley graphs generated from pseudorandom groups have [[Expander mixing lemma | strong mixing properties]]; that is, <math>\operatorname{BiCay}(\Gamma_n, S)</math> is a bipartite <math>(n, d, \lambda)</math>-graph for some <math>\lambda</math> tending to zero as <math>n</math> tends to infinity. (Recall that an <math>(n, d, \lambda)</math> graph is a graph with <math>n</math> vertices, each with degree <math>d</math>, whose adjacency matrix has a second largest eigenvalue of at most <math>\lambda.</math>)

In fact, it can be shown that for any <math>c</math>-quasirandom group <math>\Gamma</math>, the number of solutions to <math>xy=z</math> with <math>x \in X</math>, <math>y \in Y</math>, and <math>z \in Z</math> is approximately equal to what one might expect if <math>S</math> was chosen randomly; that is, approximately equal to <math>\tfrac{| X | | Y | | Z |}{| \Gamma |}.</math> This result follows from a direct application of the [[expander mixing lemma]].

== Examples ==

There are several notable families of quasirandom groups. In each case, the quasirandomness properties are most easily verified by checking the dimension of its smallest non-trivial representation.

* The projective special linear groups <math>\operatorname{PSL}(2, p)</math> for prime <math>p</math> form a sequence of quasirandom groups, since a classic result of [[Frobenius]] states that its smallest non-trivial representation has dimension at least <math>\tfrac{1}{2}(p-1).</math> In fact, these groups are the groups with the largest known minimal non-trivial representation, as a function of group order.
* The [[alternating groups]] <math>(A_n)</math> are quasirandom, since its smallest non-trivial representation has dimension <math>n-1.</math>
* Any sequence of non-cyclic [[simple groups]] with increasing order is quasirandom, since its smallest non-trivial representation has dimension at least <math>\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\log n}</math>, where <math>n</math> is the order of the group.<ref name="g"/>
